answers:
1. It was our existing SCADA pressure sensors, so we bought no new hardware. I don't have the exact number of points or how often they log, and I'm not sure what they were originally collected for, so I'd skip that detail.

2. We ran the pressure data through a model that sent alerts when something looked off. The first big catch was a major main leak under an elementary school, which our field tech Carlos Ruiz traced using those alerts.

3. It took 18 months to go from 14% to 9%, and it saves about 410 million gallons a year. The whole project cost $85,000. I don't have a dollar figure for the savings, and I don't have anything on other factors contributing, so I wouldn't claim it was all the pressure analysis.

4. In the first few months about 30% of the alerts were false positives, which was a pain. Honestly, I don't think the machine learning was essential. I think simple threshold rules got us most of the gains, and I'd tell other utilities to start there.

5. I'm Dr. Naomi Fischer, and I've been at Mesa Valley Water Authority for 12 years. I've got a PhD from Arizona State.

<final>
Finding Leaks with Pressure Data We Already Had

Abstract

Mesa Valley Water Authority found leaks using the SCADA pressure sensors it already had, so it bought no new hardware. We ran the pressure data through a model that sent alerts when something looked off. The first big catch was a major main leak under an elementary school, which field tech Carlos Ruiz traced using those alerts.

Over 18 months, non-revenue water fell from 14% to 9%, saving about 410 million gallons a year. The whole project cost $85,000. We can't say how much of that drop came from the pressure analysis alone.

In the first few months, about 30% of the alerts were false positives, which was a pain. I also don't think the machine learning was essential. Simple threshold rules got us most of the gains, and I'd tell other utilities to start there.

Short Bio

Dr. Naomi Fischer is a senior engineer at Mesa Valley Water Authority and has been there 12 years. She has a PhD from Arizona State.
</final>

We ran the pressure data through a model that sent alerts when something looked off. The first big catch was a major main leak under an elementary school, which field tech Carlos Ruiz traced using those alerts.

In the first few months, about 30% of the alerts were false positives, which was a pain. I also don't think the machine learning was essential. Simple threshold rules got us most of the gains, and I'd tell other utilities to start there.
